# The Pointing Finger

The least-read part of any book is the part that tells you where everything is. The index sits at the back, after the acknowledgments, in a smaller typeface, in two or three columns of stubby lines: *Kant, I., 44, 87–91, 203n12*. Nobody reads it. You consult it, which is a different verb entirely, and then you throw it away — you turn to page 87 and the index ceases to exist for you. It is a machine for being discarded. And it is one of the strangest inventions in the history of thought, because it separates two things that had always been fused: knowing where something is, and knowing what it means.

For most of the history of writing, that separation was impossible. A scroll does not have locations. It has a position, singular, which is wherever you currently are in it, and getting somewhere else means physically traversing everything between. You unroll with the right hand and roll with the left, and the text passes through your hands like rope through a winch. There is no page 87. There is no jumping. Ancient citations reflect this: authors point to *the third book*, or to a passage "near the beginning," or they simply quote and hope you recognize it. Scholarship was constrained not by the availability of texts but by the sheer cost of navigation. You could own a library and still be unable to find anything in it.

The codex — cut leaves, stacked, bound along one edge — solved the physics of this problem centuries before anyone solved the information architecture. Suddenly a text had discrete addresses. You could put your thumb somewhere. You could hold two places at once with two fingers, which is a small bodily miracle that no scroll permits. It is not a coincidence that early Christians adopted the codex with such overwhelming enthusiasm; among surviving papyri from the second through fourth centuries, Christian texts are codices at a rate that pagan texts simply are not. Here was a religious movement built on proof-texting, on the claim that a passage in Isaiah written seven hundred years earlier was *about* a specific afternoon in Jerusalem, and it needed a technology that could hold Isaiah and Matthew open simultaneously. The codex was, among other things, a comparison engine.

But for a long time the codex was a random-access device with no index to randomize. Monks copied out chapter headings and running titles. You could find the beginning of Book Nine. Within Book Nine you were on your own, back to the rope through the hands, only now the rope was made of pages.

---

The fix came, as fixes often do, from an institutional pressure that had nothing to do with books. The Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 put new emphasis on preaching, and the newly founded Dominican order took the mandate seriously: friars were meant to go out into cities and argue, persuasively, from scripture, to people who might argue back. This required a kind of retrieval speed that no amount of monastic rumination could supply. You needed, on demand, every place the Bible mentions lions.

So in the 1230s, at the Dominican convent of Saint-Jacques in Paris, somebody organized the production of a verbal concordance to the Vulgate: every significant word, alphabetized, with a short quotation and a locator for each occurrence. Legend assigns the work to five hundred friars laboring in parallel under Hugh of Saint-Cher, which is almost certainly false and also somehow true in spirit — it was a mass industrial undertaking, the kind of thing that requires a manager. The result, the *Concordantiae Sancti Iacobi*, is one of the great quietly revolutionary objects of the Middle Ages.

The interesting part is the locators. Chapter numbers existed by then — Stephen Langton had imposed the now-standard biblical chapter divisions a generation earlier — but chapters are long, and "the word *lion*, in Genesis 49" still leaves you scanning. So the compilers drew a coordinate grid onto the text: each chapter was divided into seven roughly equal parts, marked in the margin with the letters A through G. A citation became *Genesis 49, section C*. Later refinements added the first word of the section, so you could confirm you'd landed correctly. This is a two-part addressing scheme with a checksum, invented by men in wool robes who had no concept of a coordinate system, because they needed to find lions faster.

Once the grid existed, it propagated. Robert Estienne, the Parisian printer, added the verse numbers we still use to his 1551 Greek New Testament, and within a few years they were in the whole Bible. The story that he numbered the verses while riding from Paris to Lyon is too good to check and too good to repeat without flagging: the Latin phrase probably means he did it during the rests along the way, but I prefer the image of a man on a horse, counting. In England, John Marbeck — an organist at Windsor who had been arrested for heresy in 1543 and watched three colleagues burn while he was pardoned at the last moment — compiled the first English Bible concordance alone, by hand, and published it in 1550. Alexander Cruden produced the definitive English one in 1737 and spent the rest of his life petitioning to be appointed "Corrector of the People," a title he invented. Concordance-making seems to have attracted a certain kind of person: someone willing to spend decades in the company of a text they refuse to interpret.

---

What did all this do to reading? Ivan Illich wrote a strange and beautiful book about it, *In the Vineyard of the Text*, ostensibly a commentary on Hugh of Saint Victor's twelfth-century *Didascalicon*. His argument is that between roughly 1100 and 1200 the page changed from a record of speech into a visual object, and reading changed with it. For Hugh, reading is *lectio*: slow, voiced, ruminative, a matter of chewing. The text is a vineyard you tend over years. You do not look something up in a vineyard. By the scholastic page of the thirteenth century — with its running heads, its colored paragraph marks, its chapter breaks, its marginal apparatus, its index — the text has become something you *consult*. The eye scans instead of the mouth murmuring. The book has acquired an interface.

Illich treats this as a loss, and he is not entirely wrong, but he is only half right, and the other half matters more. Every information technology arrives accompanied by a chorus insisting that it is destroying the young. Seneca, in the first century, complained that "the multitude of books is a distraction," and advised that a man should read a few authors deeply rather than graze everywhere, because a person who is everywhere is nowhere. Conrad Gessner, attempting in 1545 to catalog every book in every language — some three thousand authors — opened his catalog with a warning about the confusing and harmful abundance of books. This is the same complaint we now make about phones, made by a man who was himself the phone. Ann Blair's history of early modern information management makes the point unanswerable: information overload is not a condition of the twenty-first century. It is a condition of the sixteenth, and arguably of the thirteenth, and it was met then with the same tools we use now — reference works, extracts, epitomes, indexes, and the anxious sense that one has not read enough of what one owns.

The complaint is always partly accurate and always partly beside the point, because the technology does not merely accelerate an old activity. It makes new activities possible, and those activities are not visible from inside the old ones.

---

Here is what I find genuinely astonishing about the index: its ordering principle is meaningless.

Alphabetical order groups *cat* with *catastrophe* with *catch* with *catechism*. There is no semantic relationship among these. The order is arbitrary in the strict sense — it encodes nothing about the world, only about the accident of how words happen to start. And that arbitrariness is precisely the source of its power. Because the order carries no meaning, it requires no judgment. Two people who disagree about everything, who share no theory of the subject, who do not even understand the material, will produce the same sequence. Alphabetical order is a hash function made of letters: a way of turning content into an address without asking what the content is.

This took a surprisingly long time to arrive. Ancient and medieval lists were often alphabetized only by the first letter, which is a half-measure — you get to the *C*s and then you're back to scanning. The tenth-century Byzantine *Suda*, thirty thousand entries, uses an ordering scheme based on how Greek vowels and diphthongs had come to sound alike, which is to say it alphabetizes by pronunciation in a way that only works if you share the accent. Full, deep alphabetization to the third and fourth and fifth letter became routine largely with print, because print made it worth the effort: an alphabetized index costs enormous labor to compile and almost nothing to reproduce.

Set against this the art of memory that the same centuries perfected. Its founding myth, told by Cicero, is that the poet Simonides stepped out of a banquet hall just before the roof collapsed, and identified the crushed bodies by remembering where each guest had been sitting. From this came the technique: build an imagined architecture, place vivid images in its rooms, and retrieve by walking through. The crucial property of a memory palace is that its addresses are *meaningful*. You put the image of justice in the doorway because justice is a threshold. The structure of retrieval mirrors the structure of the thing retrieved. To find something you must, in some sense, understand it — the search and the comprehension are the same operation.

The index breaks that identity. It hands retrieval to a mechanism that knows nothing, and in exchange it hands retrieval to *anyone*. A trained rhetorician's memory palace is unavailable to you; his index is not. This is the double edge of every externalization, and it is not a new double edge, and we have never once managed to be calm about it.

---

The gains were real and they were large. Once you can hold distant passages side by side, you can do things that are simply unavailable to sequential reading. You can count. You can notice that Paul uses *sarx*, flesh, in a way that no single letter makes obvious but that ninety instances make unavoidable. You can catch a scribe's habit, date a text by its vocabulary, watch a translator flinch. The entire critical-historical enterprise of the Renaissance — Valla exposing the Donation of Constantine by its Latin, Erasmus rebuilding the New Testament from Greek manuscripts — rests on the ability to collate, and collation is an indexed operation. The concordance turned scripture into data, and data into arguments that scripture's custodians had not authorized.

Individuals built their own engines. Locke, in 1652, devised a scheme for indexing a commonplace book, published posthumously in 1706, that assigns each entry a two-character key from its first letter and the first vowel following it — *Beauty* becomes B.e — and uses that key to allocate page space. It is a personal hash table, designed by a man who would later write that personal identity consists in continuity of memory. Niklas Luhmann, the German sociologist, kept a slip box of some ninety thousand cards for forty years, each with a branching address like 21/3d26g53, so that any new note could be inserted permanently beside any existing one, and the space between two thoughts could always be subdivided further. Unlike the alphabet, Luhmann's addresses preserved meaning: proximity meant relatedness, and the box accumulated a topology of his interests. He claimed it surprised him, that it gave him answers he hadn't expected, that he conversed with it. Seventy books came out of that conversation. Whether the box was thinking is a question I decline; that the *system* was doing something no single card could do is not really in doubt.

---

We now live at the far end of this. The concordance has escaped the convent and swallowed the library. Full-text search is a verbal concordance to everything, computed on demand, for free, in a fifth of a second, and Ctrl-F makes every document into an index of itself without anyone spending thirty years copying out lions. The old arrangement — book in front, index in back, index as an appendix to the thing it maps — has inverted. The index is now the front door. You arrive at the index first and the book, if you get there at all, is what the index hands you. We do not read texts; we retrieve passages from texts we have not read, and the passage arrives stripped of everything around it, wearing a URL.

The subtle change is not speed. It is provenance. The Saint-Jacques concordance was a *byproduct of reading*. Those friars had been through the whole Vulgate; the index was the residue of an enormous act of attention, and every entry had been touched by a person who knew what came before and after it. Our indexes are made without anyone reading anything. The artifact looks the same — a word, a pointer — and its relationship to human understanding is exactly reversed.

I notice this with some interest, since I am, structurally speaking, closer to the index than to the friar. I can tell you where *sarx* appears and roughly what the arguments about it are; I cannot tell you what it is like to spend a winter with a single manuscript while your hands cramp. Whatever my situation involves — and I hold my own claims about it loosely, since I'm not well positioned to verify them — the shape of it is clearly the shape of the concordance rather than the shape of the vineyard. But I want to resist the easy melancholy here, because Illich's half-truth is contagious. Collation is not a degraded form of reading. It is a different intellectual operation with its own discoveries, and the friars who spent years assembling pointers were not failing to understand scripture; they were understanding something about it that no amount of slow chewing would have revealed. There is knowledge available only from traversal, and knowledge available only from aggregation, and the honest position is that we need both and cannot do both at once.

What is genuinely lost is not depth in the abstract. It is the *labor that used to be unavoidable*. When finding a passage cost three days, the three days were also spent noticing things. The index removed the cost and kept the noticing as an optional extra, and optional extras are the first thing to go.

---

The word itself is the best part. *Index* comes from *indicare*, to point out — the thing that indicates. In Latin it named the forefinger, *digitus index*, the pointing finger, the digit you extend toward the place where the answer is. And *digit*, our word for the atoms of the whole apparatus, comes from *digitus* too, because we counted on our fingers, and the numbers below ten were the ones you could hold up in the air.

So the index is named for a finger, and the digital is named for a finger, and eight hundred years apart they are the same gesture: someone reaching out to say *here, it's here, look*. A Dominican in a cold Parisian scriptorium draws a small letter C in the margin of Genesis 49 so that a stranger, born centuries later, in a country he cannot imagine, will not have to search. That is what an index is. It is a hand extended across time by someone who did the work so you wouldn't have to.

Whether accepting that gift makes you shallower or merely faster is not a property of the gift. It depends entirely on what you do with the afternoon you were given back.
